entities.summary:
Random House, founded in 1925 by Bennett Cerf and Donald Klopfer in New York City, is the world's largest trade book publisher and has published some of the 20th century's most important literary works including James Joyce's Ulysses, William Faulkner's novels, and Toni Morrison's Beloved. Random House's 1933 victory in the US Customs battle over importing Joyce's Ulysses — judge John Woolsey's ruling that Ulysses was not obscene — is the most important legal ruling in American publishing history for literary freedom.

Cerf and Klopfer bought Modern Library (a reprint series) from Boni & Liveright in 1925, naming their new company 'Random House' because they wanted to publish books 'at random.' The Ulysses obscenity battle — fought specifically so Random House could publish the American edition — and Woolsey's 1933 ruling opened American literature to frank discussion of sexuality that had been prohibited. Bennett Cerf subsequently appeared on What's My Line (1952-1967) becoming television's most recognizable publisher.

Random House's 20th-century list included William Faulkner, John Updike, Truman Capote, Robert Penn Warren, and Gore Vidal (American literary division), along with reference works including American College Dictionary. Random House merged with Penguin in 2013 creating Penguin Random House (PRH), now the world's largest trade publisher with annual revenues over $4 billion, publishing approximately 15,000 new titles per year across 300 imprints and 20 countries.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Random House's 1933 victory in the Ulysses obscenity case — establishing that literary art cannot be judged by its frankness about sexuality — is the most consequential ruling in American publishing history for literary freedom.
